name: Height-increasing supplements
lead: Height-increasing supplements are over-the-counter products, typically vitamin, mineral, amino-acid or herbal blends, marketed with the claim that they help people grow taller or reach their genetic height potential. They are discussed in height-focused looksmaxxing communities, where users ask whether growth pills work for teenagers or adults.[1]

Reference sources describe height as strongly heritable (60 to 80 percent in twin studies) and influenced by childhood nutrition and health, and report that chronic malnutrition can stunt growth.[2] The medical treatment for short stature described in reference sources is prescription growth hormone, which is given under specialist care.[3] No published trial of a marketed height supplement in healthy people was located for this article.

paras: Products sold under this heading are generally multi-ingredient formulas. A looksmax.org thread on the subject quotes material from a height-advice website describing growth supplements and guides alongside stretching content, and one replier in the thread describes the supplements as vitamins that target what supports growth without addressing a root cause, and as costly with results that take a long time to show.[1]

Wikipedia reports that genetics accounts for most variation in height within a population, and that nutrition, protein intake and overall health shape growth in childhood and adolescence.[2] It states that females generally stop growing at about 15 to 16 and males at about 18 to 19.[2] Because supplements are marketed to both teenagers and adults, how much any product could matter depends on remaining growth potential, which the sources do not quantify for supplements.

Wikipedia's article on idiopathic short stature describes growth hormone as the main medical treatment, estimates that it may move a child from about the 1st to the 10th percentile at a cost that can reach $100,000 or more, and records ethical and economic debate about its use.[3] The article does not discuss over-the-counter height supplements.[3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, height supplements appear in threads asking whether growth pills help teens or adults, often alongside discussion of stretching and other height methods.[1]

claims.claim: Growth supplements can help people grow taller or reach full potential.
claims.believers: Marketers and some forum posters describe vitamin-type formulas as supporting the nutrients growth requires; at least one poster says he has considered them.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia attributes variation in height mainly to genetics and childhood nutrition, and no published trial located for this article has tested a marketed height supplement.[2]

claims.claim: Supplements are too expensive and slow to be worth it.
claims.believers: A forum replier says they are costly, take a long time to show results and are just vitamins that do not tackle the root cause.[1]
claims.experts: No price or outcome studies of such products were located.

card.summary: OTC pills sold to make you taller; height is mostly genetic and no trial backs them for adults.
card.note: No published trials of marketed height supplements were found.

quick.overview:
Height supplements are over-the-counter blends marketed to help people grow taller. Forum users ask whether they help teens or adults, and some call them costly and slow.

Reference sources describe height as mostly genetic and shaped by childhood nutrition. No trial of a marketed height supplement was found.
quick.mechanism: Marketers say the vitamins and minerals support the nutrients growth needs. Sources describe nutrition as affecting growth in childhood, but none tests these products.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to height supplements were located. Prescription growth hormone is a separate, medically supervised treatment.
